title: Police clear encampment on Williamson and Baldwin streets in Madison - Spectrum News
text: MADISON, Wis. — Police cleared the encampment on Williamson Street and Baldwin Street on Tuesday morning. The occupation of the streets began after police shot and killed Corey Ruiz less than two weeks ago. Authorities came in with bobcats and other heavy machinery to begin clearing barricades, furniture and tents at the site around 4:30 a.m. The city said it did not want to get law enforcement involved but some protesters refused to clear, with some throwing objects at vehicles and lighting fires in the street. That's when the Madison Police Department stepping in. It corralled protesters in the center of the intersection and arrested several people who were trying to prevent the memorial for Ruiz from being taken down. According to the city, the streets were officially back open as of 9 a.m. All city barricades and signage were removed from the area. Supporters of the encampment and memorial criticized the city for how the entire situation was handled. “They could have just been direct and said we’re going to give you 48 hours to move out and then everybody could’ve been given a timeline, nobody was ever given a clear timeline, all they kept doing was throwing vouches, hotel vouchers at the houseless community, less than half of the people here were houseless," said Shadayra Kilfoy-Flores. The latest development comes after Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway called for an end to the encampment, with leaders saying a peaceful end was the best path forward. Rhodes-Conway issued a new video message on Tuesday following the encampment being cleared. She said the city is fully cooperating with the investigation. "As soon as we are allowed to under state law, the police department will provide all relevant materials to the Office of the Independent Monitor for their investigation,” she said, addressing claims last week by the Monitor that MPD was not cooperating with turning over materials. The mayor said the decision to clear the encampment was not made lightly, but there was much to consider, with local businesses and residents caught in the middle of what she called "an increasingly volatile situation." "I ask that if you truly care about building a better future, you allow local businesses to stay open, residents to freely access their homes, and the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin Streets to stay open. Let's focus our energy on the hard work of sustainable change. Holding government accountable for progress should not mean harming the community we all share," she said in the video. Police remained at the scene on Tuesday. The city has also sectioned off a portion of the sidewalk on Baldwin Street as a designated memorial site for Ruiz. The city said those looking to pick up their belongings could do so at the parking lot of Demetral Park; city staff will be there until midnight. As of Tuesday afternoon, about one third of the items had been picked up. Kaitlynn Rouse was one of several people who helps people sift through the various items taken from the encampment. She said she thinks what the city did Tuesday showed a lack of respect.  “I think there should have been a lot more care and empathy when it came to, at the very least, the people and the people’s resources and items," she said. Both Rouse and Kilfoy-Flores said this was just another example of the growing rift between city leaders and the people of Madison. “They’re against the community members who are grieving, in pain, and just seeing it as a nuisance instead of people who just care about their community," said Rouse. "We were starting to get past the anger part, and then there’s healing, but now we’re back to square one,” said Kilfoy-Flores. While the encampment may be gone, protesters said they won't stop fighting for accountability in Ruiz's death.

title: UPDATE: Protestors return to former encampment site in Madison - WTMJ
text: UPDATE 8/4/26 at 4:00p.m. – Protestors have returned to the intersection of Willy and Baldwin Streets in Madison hours after police had cleared out the encampment in the street. The barricades that had blocked off the street have not returned but protestors could be seen walking in circles around the intersection while police monitored close by. This is a developing story; more information will be added as it becomes available. MADISON, Wis. – A protest encampment blocking off a Madison intersection for nearly two weeks is cleared for traffic once again. But those occupying the site at Willy and Baldwin Streets where police last month shot and killed 38-year-old Corey Ruiz did not leave quietly. Police made at least 10 arrests as protestors hurled rocks and lit multiple fires near the encampment that formed in the street in the days following Ruiz’s death. title: Video Message from Mayor Rhodes-Conway - City of Madison, WI
text: For Immediate Release August 4, 2026 "Good morning, I'm Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway.  I want to start by saying that the death of Corey Ruiz is, tragically, another wake up call for Madison. Even one community member killed during interactions with the police is too many. The grief, anger, and frustration are real and I feel it, too. I want to be clear that the City is fully cooperating with the independent investigation conducted by the Wisconsin Department of Justice, and will respect whatever decisions the District Attorney makes regarding charges for the officers involved. As soon as we are allowed to under state law, the police department will provide all relevant materials to the Office of the Independent Monitor for their investigation.   There is more work to be done at the City level to prevent this from happening again - work to build on the success of our CARES program in diverting calls away from police, work on police policy and training, and more. We need reform at the state level as well. I know it's unsatisfying to hear that change takes time, and that these investigations and processes require patience. But these things do take time and many of the changes needed are not in City government's control.   For nearly two weeks, I and City staff have been working day and night to peacefully resolve the occupation of Williamson and Baldwin without law enforcement intervention. The City has committed to maintaining space for members of the community to gather and grieve, and we stand ready to do that work in collaboration with the family and the community. But that work could not begin while city streets were occupied, local businesses were on the verge of closing, and residents in the Marquette neighborhood were caught in the middle of an increasingly volatile situation.   A challenge of the last two weeks was that there was not one leader, one group, or one coalition that represented the people occupying the intersection. What is deeply regrettable is that many vulnerable people were caught in the middle, which is why the City spent considerable time and effort finding emergency solutions — efforts that succeeded in helping dozens of unsheltered people and families. We were doing this work before the occupation, and we will continue to do this work moving forward.  This morning, the City of Madison opened the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin. The work was led by non-law enforcement staff from multiple City agencies. Our goal was to clear the barricades, preserve personal belongings and memorial materials, and open the street up to normal traffic. The CARES Team and members of the Violence Prevention Unit were there from the beginning to assist.  Unfortunately, as City staff cleared the area, rocks and other items were thrown at City employees and two fires were set; as a result, law enforcement was called in to stabilize the scene, and a small number of individuals were arrested. Again, multiple efforts and calls to end the occupation peacefully were made but ultimately ignored.  The 50 or so unsheltered individuals who were onsite were given the option to stay in hotels and were offered transportation there. A significant majority decided to do so and around 10 people were also placed in hotel rooms yesterday. This effort was done with as much compassion as possible under less-than-ideal circumstances. Those with personal belongings left at the site can pick them up at Demetral Field.   Again, the decision to invoke this option was not made lightly and was only made after almost two weeks of trying to resolve the situation peacefully, and voluntarily, with the people occupying the site.  There are many hard conversations to come and I look forward to us coming together as a community to have them. I ask that if you truly care about building a better future, you allow local businesses to stay open, residents to freely access their homes, and the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin Streets to stay open. Let's focus our energy on the hard work of sustainable change. Holding government accountable for progress should not mean harming the community we all share.   Thank you, Madison. We are a strong and compassionate community. Together, we can support each other. Together, we can work towards change. Together we can get through this. title: Madison officials, cops clear protesters from encampment at police shooting site - wisconsinexaminer.com

Videos posted to social media show a chaotic scene at which police grappled with protesters and deployed pepper spray. City officials also towed away the replica George Floyd fist statue that was brought to the intersection last week. Dylan Brogan, a spokesperson for the city, said the city planned to let non-police city staff lead the effort. “The plan was for this to be led by non-law enforcement city agencies,” he said, adding that the unhoused people staying at the site would be given the opportunity to stay in a hotel and that people’s belongings would be available for pickup at Demetral Field, located about 2 miles northeast of the protest encampment site. “The message was delivered loudly that people had to get their things together.” The city announced that the intersection was open to traffic at 9 a.m. In a statement released Monday evening, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway warned that the encampment would be shut down on Tuesday — stating that Ruiz was “no longer at the center of the current crisis our city faces.” “For almost two weeks now, City of Madison staff and elected leaders have been on the ground and communicating to and through community leaders to peacefully resolve extremely complex, emotionally fraught circumstances that started with the police taking the life of Corey Ruiz,” Rhodes-Conway stated. “Countless efforts have been made to convince people that the occupation of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is counterproductive.
